name: mass_of_a_steel_cube
why: «How much does this part weigh» is one of the two questions asked before ordering material. A 100x100x20 cube makes 200,000 mm3; the AISI 304 of the SOLIDWORKS library has a density of 8000 kg/m3, so exactly 1.6 kg. None of the three numbers is rounded: it is a calculation that has to add up.
_already_seen_red: This case has already fired, on 15/9/2026, the first time it was run: «density_kg_m3 1 (expected 8000)». `IMassProperty` changes its answers depending on what it was asked before -- once `Volume` or `SurfaceArea` has been read on that object, `Density` becomes 1 and the mass comes out EIGHT THOUSAND TIMES lighter, with volume, area and centroid all right beside it. The operation now uses a new object for every number, and this line is what keeps it true.
_why_the_recompute: the mass arrives twice -- the one from SOLIDWORKS and the one redone by hand as volume times density -- and the deviation between the two is an expectation in its own right. If one day one of the two measurements were in units different from those it declares, this line would say so: a factor of a thousand does not hide in a difference.

expect.tolerance_why: the volume is read in cubic metres and multiplied by a billion
2*(100*100) + 4*(100*20) = 28,000; the area is read in square metres
it is the density that the SOLIDWORKS library gives to AISI 304
200,000 mm3 times 8000 kg/m3 = 1.6 kg: the thousandth is the rounding of the answer
the two routes must give the same number, not a similar one
the centroid is read in metres; the plate is centred in X and Y and goes from z = 0 to z = 20

expect.why: whoever reads the answer may never have seen the description of the operation
